description: Savor the rich and fiery flavors of this authentic Vegetarian Mapo Tofu, a beloved Sichuan dish reimagined for plant-based enjoyment. Silken tofu cubes are simmered in a deeply aromatic, spicy, and savory sauce, delivering a delightful "ma la" numbing sensation. This hearty and satisfying recipe brings the essence of Chinese cuisine to your table, perfect for a comforting and vibrant meal.

ingredients.notes: optional, substitute with more broth for strict vegetarian
green parts thinly sliced, for garnish

instructions.title: Prepare Tofu and Aromatics
instructions.text: Gently drain the tofu and cut it into 1-inch cubes. If using silken tofu, you may blanch it in hot water for 5 minutes and drain to firm it up slightly and remove beany taste. Prepare ginger, garlic, fermented black beans, and slice scallions.

instructions.title: Bloom Spices
instructions.text: Heat vegetable oil in a wok or large pan over medium heat. Add the ground Sichuan peppercorns (if using whole, toast them first, then remove and grind) and chili flakes (if using). Stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant, then remove the peppercorns if you prefer less texture, leaving the oil infused.

instructions.title: Build the Flavor Base
instructions.text: Add minced ginger, garlic, and chopped fermented black beans to the aromatic oil. Stir-fry for about 1 minute until fragrant. Add the Sichuan chili bean paste and stir-fry for another 1-2 minutes until the oil turns red and fragrant.

instructions.title: Simmer the Tofu
instructions.text: Pour in the vegetable broth, soy sauce, sugar, and Shaoxing wine (if using). Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer. Carefully add the tofu cubes to the sauce. Gently push the tofu around to coat it, avoiding vigorous stirring that could break the cubes. Simmer for 5-7 minutes, allowing the tofu to absorb the flavors.

instructions.title: Thicken and Finish
instructions.text: Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir and slowly pour it into the simmering sauce while gently stirring. Continue to cook for 1-2 minutes until the sauce thickens to your desired consistency. Remove from heat and stir in the sesame oil.

instructions.title: Serve
instructions.text: Transfer the Vegetarian Mapo Tofu to a serving dish. Garnish generously with the sliced green parts of the scallions. Serve immediately with steamed white rice.

tips: For an authentic "ma la" sensation, use freshly ground Sichuan peppercorns. Toast them lightly in a dry pan before grinding to intensify their unique citrusy, numbing flavor.
Adjust the spice level by varying the amount of Doubanjiang and chili flakes. For a deeper umami, consider adding a pinch of mushroom powder or a splash of vegetarian oyster sauce.

Mapo Tofu is best served immediately and hot with freshly steamed white rice. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, but the tofu's texture may soften further.
article:
Mapo Tofu. The name alone evokes images of fiery red, bubbling chili oil, and tender silken tofu, a dish celebrated for its bold flavors and tantalizing textures. Originating from Sichuan, China, this iconic creation captivates taste buds worldwide with its unique "ma la" (numbing and spicy) sensation. While traditionally made with meat, the culinary world has embraced equally compelling plant-based versions. For those exploring Chinese vegetarian cuisine, recreating this classic without meat is not only possible but spectacularly delicious. Get ready to dive into the world of **Vegetarian Mapo Tofu**, a dish that proves meat is entirely optional when delivering authentic Sichuan flavor. This guide will help you master this fiery, flavorful, and satisfying dish.

## What is Vegetarian Mapo Tofu?

At its core, Mapo Tofu is a vibrant celebration of tofu, chili, and Sichuan peppercorns. The traditional dish features soft tofu in a spicy, oily sauce, typically flavored with fermented broad bean paste (doubanjiang), fermented black beans, chili flakes, and Sichuan peppercorns. For the **Vegetarian Mapo Tofu** version, animal protein is omitted, allowing the complex spices and delicate tofu to shine. This adaptation retains all signature characteristics: the fiery heat, the distinctive numbing sensation, the savory depth from doubanjiang, and the soft, wobbly tofu texture. It's a cornerstone of Chinese vegetarian cooking, demonstrating how traditional dishes can be deliciously reimagined, offering a deeply satisfying and naturally protein-rich meal without compromise.
